questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Oxidation** (in terms of oxygen) is the **gain of oxygen** by a substance. Example: in equation I, copper gains oxygen to form copper(II) oxide.

(ii) **Reduction** (in terms of hydrogen) is the **gain of hydrogen** by a substance. Example: $\mathrm{N_2 + 3H_2 \rightarrow 2NH_3}$, where nitrogen gains hydrogen. (Reduction is also the loss of oxygen, as for CuO in equation II.)

(i) In equation I the **reducing agent is copper, Cu**. It gains oxygen (it is oxidised) and in doing so it reduces the oxygen ($\mathrm{O_2}$ is the oxidising agent).

(ii) In equation II the **oxidising agent is copper(II) oxide, CuO**. It gives its oxygen to hydrogen (so hydrogen is oxidised to water) and is itself reduced to copper.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Determine the oxidation state of,

(i) Copper in Cu

(ii) Oxygen in $\mathrm{H_2O}$ *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Copper in Cu (the free element, as printed) has oxidation state **0**: the oxidation state of any uncombined element is zero. (If the compound CuO was meant, copper would be $+2$ because oxygen is $-2$ and the compound is neutral.)

(ii) In $\mathrm{H_2O}$ hydrogen is $+1$ and the molecule is neutral, so $2(+1) + x = 0$ and the oxidation state of oxygen is $x = $ **$-2$**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
State whether each of these reactions involves oxidation or reduction or both.

(i) $\mathrm{Al^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Al}$

(ii) $2\mathrm{O^{2-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{O_2} + 4\mathrm{e^-}$

(iii) $2\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O}$ *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) $\mathrm{Al^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Al}$: **reduction** (aluminium ions gain electrons).

(ii) $2\mathrm{O^{2-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{O_2} + 4\mathrm{e^-}$: **oxidation** (oxide ions lose electrons; the charge balances: $-4 = -4$).

(iii) $2\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O}$: **both oxidation and reduction** (a redox reaction). Hydrogen gains oxygen (oxidation, oxidation state $0 \rightarrow +1$) while oxygen is reduced (oxidation state $0 \rightarrow -2$).
